results.finding: sections, unit counts and unit forms match the spec

All 33 unit summaries agree with the controlling idea of the spec paragraph each is aligned to (p01-p12, p14-p34). The research unit (p10) also carries the walkthrough method from the author's record, which the spec's evidence for p10 declares; the pattern units (p14, p17, p20) give user, test and limit as declared.

The outliner marked two units. Setting the Scene ¶2 (p04) gives why the report counted output and why the proposed mandate was declined; both are one analysis of the scene, the same single controlling idea the spec states for p04 (the report counted output and the easy remedy would have hidden the reason the count was low). Worked Example ¶5 (p27) gives the lasting change and the open question; its first sentence announces both ('one lasting change and one open question') and the spec's controlling idea for p27 holds both as what the review left. Neither is a paragraph with two unrelated ideas. Introduction ¶2 and Checklist ¶1 carry two elements by house design and were not marked.

Every unit serves a supporting claim: the scene and the stance S1 and S6, the developer-experience units S2, the funding units S3, the thin-platform units S4, the roadmap units S5, the anti-pattern and mandate units S6 and S1, the worked example S2-S6 applied to the opening case, and the AI units apply S1 and S2 to a new kind of user. No unit is an orphan.

Each of the six tables is introduced and read in the prose around it (the scene table by 'The first column below comes from...' and 'Nothing in the report was false'; the measures table of the worked example by 'The table gave one finding'; the roadmap table by 'The table gives the three items and his decisions'). Figure 1 has a caption and three sentences giving each question and its source. There are no direct quotations; paraphrased sources name author and work. The declared evidence items are all present with what they show, including the Corvane ledger facts, the two research papers marked as supplements cited from their abstracts, and the test that would confirm the speculative AI claim.

All declared transitions were read at their boundaries and express the declared relationship: p02 (problem to solution, 'what it does for those users'), the nine section openings (e.g. 'What Corvane's report lacked was its users', 'With a measure in hand', 'A load worth funding still leaves open how much to build', 'After the first version', 'Corvane took the slower way'), the paragraph transitions inside sections (e.g. 'One consequence of the product stance', 'The infrastructure-team model does without that evidence', 'The selection is mine, but this way of measuring is not', 'The second row does not make a mandate always wrong', 'The table gave one finding', 'The fix was thin') and the phrase-form transitions of the conclusion. The AI section opens with the label sentence the spec's evidence prescribes and makes its link ('users of internal platforms alongside people') in the next sentence; p29 states its contrast in content (agents as users against agents making it cheaper to avoid the platform) although the connective is 'also'.

Both flow readers describe the declared organisation: a case poses the problem, then stance, measure and three patterns in prerequisite order (fund, build thin, plan the next versions), then failures and the mandate exception, the case worked through, and AI as a coda. Neither marked any section's position unclear, neither had to go back to an earlier section, and both say no section should move. No point was reported by both readers and rated (a) by both, so nothing is corroborated; the local stumbles follow as separate results.

results.quote: Read the three together, and ask the teams that stayed away.
results.finding: Five measures were just given and the paragraph speaks of 'both' sources, so the reader has to count back to find which three are meant. Flow reader A (rated a) was left unsure which set is the core, because the worked example's report later leads with a different three (adoption by choice, adopters' lead time, time to a first release) than the synthesis names (adoption, lead time, friction). Flow reader B reported the same sentence but rated it b (resolved by counting back), so the point is not corroborated as a lost thread.

results.quote: Together they are the **load** a platform exists to remove, and the rest of the chapter uses the word in that sense.
results.finding: Load is fixed as waiting plus what a team has to know, but the funding section's example of a load statement ('about twelve engineer-days a quarter keeping their own deployment scripts working') is maintenance effort, which is neither; flow reader B (rated a) had to assume that effort counts as load. Flow reader A noticed only that 'load' is used before this definition and did not stumble. One reader only. Both the definition and the example are in the spec, but a clause in the draft saying that upkeep effort counts would settle it.

results.draft_locus: Worked Example: Corvane's Platform Review of 2026 ¶4
results.quote: Seven of the eleven teams of 2024 kept their own scripts for setting up a test environment, and the newer teams copied them
results.finding: The row is presented under 'Load statement' but gives no amount and no way it was measured, which the chapter said a load statement must give; flow reader B (rated a) had to assume the incomplete statement is why the decision was only a reviewed thin version. One reader only. The row's content is taken from the spec's evidence for p26, which gives it without an amount.

results.quote: The last two rows of the table speak of what changes for the users, and that has a name.
results.finding: Only the third row of the preceding table ('adoption by choice and what changed for the adopters') speaks of what changes for users; the fourth is about what low adoption means. Both flow readers reported it (A item 8, B item 5) and both rated it b, resolved on re-reading, so it is a local inaccuracy and not a lost thread.

results.draft_locus: Pattern: Fund the Platform Against Measured Load ¶2
results.quote: Its users are the leader who approves the budget and the teams the statement names.
results.finding: Up to this point 'users' has meant the teams that use the platform; in the pattern paragraphs ('Its users are...', 'Its user is that first team') it means the users of the pattern, and 'Its' can be read as the platform's. Both flow readers reported it (A item 4, B item 6) and both rated it b.

results.draft_locus: Pattern: Start with the Thinnest Viable Platform ¶2
results.quote: At Corvane the release path runs the readiness checks for every team, and what a team's own check asserts about its own service stays with that team.
results.finding: The sentence needed two readings to separate running the checks (platform) from what a check asserts (team), and 'for every team' jars with eleven of about thirty teams being on the path. Both flow readers reported it (A item 6, B item 8) and both rated it b.

results.draft_locus: A Platform Is a Product Whose Users Are Teams ¶1
results.quote: As the introduction said, [[team-types]] decides whether an organization should have a platform team at all
results.finding: 'The introduction' can be read as the book's introduction; it means this chapter's second paragraph. Both flow readers paused on it (A item 7, B item 3) and both rated it b.

results.draft_locus: Setting the Scene: Nine Items Shipped, Eleven Teams On ¶2
results.quote: That is how the common alternative to this chapter works.
results.finding: 'The alternative to this chapter' is an odd referent (an alternative to a chapter); the next sentence, which names the infrastructure-team model, resolves it. Both flow readers reported it (A item 5, B item 4) and both rated it b.

Every term on the spec's does_not_know list is defined at or before its first use in the body: platform as a product and paved path (product section ¶1), developer experience (introduction and its own section), adoption by choice (product section ¶2), thinnest viable platform (its section ¶1), load statement (funding section ¶1), feature shop (roadmap section ¶1), shadow platform (anti-patterns ¶1). Stream-aligned team, release path, self-service, the infrastructure-team model, discovery, team API, lead time and friction are each defined in a clause where they first matter. 'Load' appears in the introduction's thesis before its definition in the developer-experience section; the plain sense and chapter 4's cognitive load carry it, and no reader reported it as unexplained (its fit with the later example is recorded under flow).

The cold reader of the introduction found none of the weak patterns: the opening is a specific scene with numbers, a bridge to the reader's own experience, a stated thesis and a roadmap. Its remark that the callouts and the second paragraph state the thesis several times concerns the house page format.

The conclusion does not merely restate the thesis, raise a new topic or apologise: it sorts the claims by how settled they are, gives a synthesis the body did not state in that form (one question asked before, during and after the work), a course of action and a hand-off.

The checklist's lead-in carries the declared synthesis ('one question asked three times: what does a named set of teams no longer have to wait for or know?'; the load statement before, the thin version during, adoption by choice with the adopters' lead time afterwards; 'A platform team that can answer needs no mandate, and a mandate does not help one that cannot') and the so-what ('judge your platform by its users' outcomes and not by its output'); the eight checks give the declared course of action, including funding each item by a load statement and asking teams that stayed away.

The closing paragraph returns to Dario Vance's question and the nine items shipped and says what the report lacked ('its users') and what the count was for ('the count began to say what the platform had done for the teams'), as the spec's callback declares.

From the introduction alone the cold reader predicted the chapter's subject, its claim and ten steps in the order the roadmap promises and the sections follow (scene, product stance, developer experience and its measures, the three patterns, failures and the place of a mandate, Corvane's review, AI), with the Corvane case as the main evidence. It did not expect cited research, which is one paragraph of the body and does not change the route.

The cold reader's answer matches the expected one: not a success on this evidence; measure adoption by choice with the adopters' lead time and reported friction (plus time to a first use and the share of uses without a request); ask the eleven teams that stayed away and treat the answers as findings about the product; do not mandate; find the cause and fix it thinly with one or two non-adopting teams so the path becomes the easier one; and change the report to lead with adoption and adopters' lead time and not features shipped.

The introduction sends the question of when a platform team is justified to team-types ('this chapter starts once the answer is yes'); the definition paragraph gives the criterion in one clause and says 'I do not repeat that argument here'; the funding pattern cites team-types for the three-team rule of thumb. The argument is not made again.

Borrowed concepts name the book and the concept: platform as a product, voluntary against mandated adoption, the leverage test, the centralization test, the feature shop, the shadow platform, migration as the platform team's work (Fournier and Nowland, Platform Engineering); the thinnest viable platform (Skelton and Pais, Team Topologies); the question before building, biased samples and triage (Hohpe, Platform Strategy); SPACE and DevEx with authors and year, said to be cited from abstracts; the walkthrough and code-enforced guardrails (Platform Engineer's Handbook). The text says the books are cited through the author's records. The three-team threshold is given as 'my rule of thumb'. Extensions are marked: the narrow definition ('The definition is mine'), 'friction is my word', 'The selection is mine', the load statement per item ('is my extension'), 'I add one condition', the first planning habit ('is my addition'), and the author's synthesis list in the conclusion.

Each of the three pattern paragraphs names its user and a test by which a reader could tell it worked: the leader who approves the budget and the named teams, with the named load re-measured a quarter or two later having fallen by more than the item cost; the first team, which keeps using the thin version after the platform engineers leave while a second team takes it up unaided; the platform lead and the teams asked, with every roadmap item naming teams and a measure that moved after shipping. Each also states where it does not fit.
